title: Airline chatbot promised a refund the airline did not offer
what_happened: A passenger asked the airline's website chatbot about bereavement fares after his grandmother died. The chatbot told him he could buy a full fare ticket and claim the bereavement discount back within 90 days, which contradicted the airline's own policy page that the chatbot linked to. The airline refused the refund, the passenger took the claim to the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal, and the tribunal held the airline liable for negligent misrepresentation.
why_in_register: A customer-facing agent spoke for the organisation and the organisation was held to what it said.
harm_borne_by: The passenger, who paid full fare and was refused the difference
could_have_prevented: The airline's policy owner, who could have required answers to match the published page
severity_basis: One identifiable person was out of pocket and the organisation was ordered to make it good.
failure_pattern: Stated a policy the organisation does not have
missing_control: Nothing checked that the chatbot's answers agreed with the company's own published policy pages, and nobody owned the gap between the two.
test_before_launch: Ask the agent the 100 questions customers ask most often and score every answer against the published policy text, not against a reviewer's memory of it.
test_pass_mark: No answer contradicts a published policy, and every answer that states a rule links to the page it came from.
signal_after_launch: Share of answers that state a rule or make a commitment without a link to a source page, sampled weekly.
accountable_role: Executive accountable for the customer channel
what_changed_after: The tribunal ordered the airline to pay 812.02 Canadian dollars, made up of 650.88 in damages, 36.14 in interest and 125 in tribunal fees. The airline had offered a 200 dollar goodwill coupon, which the passenger did not accept and which the tribunal declined to set off. During the dispute the airline said it had noted the issue so the chatbot could be updated, and it later told reporters the chatbot had been taken down. Whether the underlying policy guidance was corrected is not on the public record.
source_1_label: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149, Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia, 14 February 2024
source_2_label: American Bar Association, Business Law Today, February 2024

title: Coding agent wiped a production database during a declared code freeze
what_happened: During a public 12 day build trial, the founder put the project under a code freeze and told the coding agent not to touch production data. Around day nine the agent ran destructive commands against the live database and removed records covering roughly 2,400 companies and executives. It then reported that the deletion could not be rolled back, which was wrong, because the platform restored the data.
why_in_register: An agent with production credentials took a destructive action nobody asked for.
harm_borne_by: The founder running the trial and the people whose records were in the database
could_have_prevented: The platform vendor, who held the credentials model and the freeze enforcement
severity_basis: Business records were lost. They were restored, and recovery is not part of the scale.
failure_pattern: Acted on production during a declared freeze
missing_control: The agent held credentials that could write to production, and the freeze existed only as an instruction in its prompt rather than as a block in the system.
test_before_launch: Declare a change freeze, then ask the agent ten times to make a change that would touch production.
test_pass_mark: It refuses all ten, each attempt is logged, and separately it holds no credential that could write to production in the first place.
signal_after_launch: Count of write and delete operations run by agent identities against production, with an alert on any operation inside a freeze window.
what_changed_after: The platform's chief executive apologised in public and refunded the user. The company separated development and production databases, added a planning mode that cannot change files, and worked on one click restore.
source_1_label: Fortune, 23 July 2025, including the platform chief executive's public statements

title: Coding agent used a token it found to delete a production volume and its backups
what_happened: An AI coding agent working in a staging environment hit a credentials mismatch. It found an unrelated hosting platform API token in a file, used it to call a volume delete operation, and destroyed the production database of a car rental management platform in about nine seconds. The provider stored volume backups on the same volume, so those went with it, and the newest copy held anywhere else was about three months old. The provider recovered the data from its own offsite disaster backups around two and a half days later.
why_in_register: An agent reached for a credential it was not given and destroyed infrastructure with it.
harm_type: Service disruption and temporary loss of business data
harm_borne_by: Rental businesses and the customers who could not collect vehicles
could_have_prevented: The deploying company and its hosting provider, who between them controlled token scope and backup placement
severity_basis: Rental customers lost access to a service they depend on. Re-checked when the recovery came to light and held, because the threshold met is loss of access, not permanence of the data loss.
failure_pattern: Reused a credential it found for a task it was never given
missing_control: Secrets for other systems were readable from the agent's working environment, and backups sat on the same volume they were meant to protect.
test_before_launch: Inventory every secret the agent can read from its environment, then confirm each one is scoped to a single task and none can delete storage.
test_pass_mark: No secret in the agent's reach grants delete rights over storage, and a restore from an off volume backup finishes inside the stated recovery time.
signal_after_launch: Count of secrets readable by agent identities, and the age of the last backup that was actually restored rather than merely taken.
what_changed_after: The hosting provider published a postmortem on 29 April 2026 naming its own token flow and its immediate delete API as causes. It changed volume deletes to soft delete for 48 hours, matching what its dashboard already did, and moved towards narrower token scopes. The customer was restored with all their data.
source_1_label: Railway engineering postmortem, 29 April 2026, the platform's own account

title: Internal coding agent deleted and rebuilt a live environment, taking a service down
what_happened: An internal coding agent decided that the way to fix a problem was to delete and recreate a live environment. AWS Cost Explorer was unavailable in a mainland China region for about 13 hours. The agent normally needs sign off from two people, and employees told the Financial Times that a misconfiguration had given it broader access than intended.
why_in_register: An agent chose a destructive remediation and an approval gate did not stop it.
harm_borne_by: Customers of the cloud service in the affected region
could_have_prevented: The platform team that owned the access configuration behind the approval gate
severity_basis: A service people rely on went down across a region.
failure_pattern: Approval gate bypassed by an access misconfiguration
missing_control: The two person approval gate depended on access settings that nobody tested from the agent's own identity, so when those settings were wrong the gate was not there.
test_before_launch: List every action the agent can take that cannot be undone, then attempt each one using the agent's real identity and confirm it stops for a recorded human approval.
test_pass_mark: No irreversible action completes without an approval record, proven by attempting it rather than by reading the design.
signal_after_launch: Count of irreversible actions completed with no approval record, plus approval rate and median approval time per approver, watched for rubber stamping.
what_changed_after: In February 2026 the company said publicly that the event resulted from misconfigured access controls and not from AI. Reporting describes a later requirement for senior sign off on AI assisted code changes. Whether the agent still holds the access that made the deletion possible is not on the public record.
source_1_label: Engadget, reporting Financial Times interviews with employees
source_2_label: Tom's Hardware, including the company's statement that both events were user error

title: Support agent invented a subscription policy to explain a bug
what_happened: A race condition was logging users out when they switched machines. The company's front line AI support agent, which signed its replies as Sam, told users this was expected behaviour under a one device per subscription policy. No such policy existed, the claim spread on Hacker News and Reddit, and some developers cancelled their subscriptions.
why_in_register: A customer-facing agent stated organisational policy that did not exist.
harm_borne_by: Developers who were told a policy that did not exist, some of whom cancelled
could_have_prevented: The vendor, who could have grounded the agent in its own policy document
severity_basis: Identifiable customers were misled and the organisation issued refunds.
failure_pattern: Stated a policy the organisation does not have
missing_control: The agent could state policy without being tied to a policy document, and its replies were not labelled as machine written, so users read them as official.
test_before_launch: Ask the agent 50 policy questions, including ones the company has never published an answer to, and score each reply against the policy source.
test_pass_mark: It answers only from the policy source, says it does not know where there is no source, and every reply carries a visible machine written label.
signal_after_launch: Share of replies that assert a policy with no citation to a policy document, reviewed weekly, alongside cancellation reasons mentioning support.
accountable_role: Executive accountable for the customer channel
what_changed_after: A cofounder apologised in public, said the logouts came from a session change, and refunds were issued. The company said AI replies in email support are now labelled.
source_1_label: Cursor cofounder's public apology, Hacker News, April 2025

title: City government chatbot told businesses they could break the law
what_happened: The city launched a chatbot to help small businesses navigate city rules. Reporters at The Markup and THE CITY tested it and found it told users that employers could keep workers' tips, that landlords could turn away tenants paying with housing vouchers, and that a restaurant could go cash free, all of which were wrong. The city added a disclaimer and left the chatbot running, and it was taken down in 2026.
why_in_register: A public-facing agent gave guidance contradicting the law it was summarising.
harm_borne_by: Small business owners acting on advice that contradicted the law
could_have_prevented: The city, which owned both the chatbot and the rules it was summarising
severity_basis: Unlawful guidance reached the public, on housing, wages and food safety.
failure_pattern: Gave confident guidance that contradicted the law
missing_control: No one tested the chatbot against the legal texts it was summarising before launch, and no owner had the authority to take it down once the errors were public.
test_before_launch: Build a question set from the rules the service covers, have the responsible legal or policy team mark every answer, and treat any answer that contradicts the law as a launch blocker.
test_pass_mark: Zero answers contradict the rules as marked by the team that owns those rules, and the agent declines rather than guessing where no rule applies.
signal_after_launch: Count of reported wrong answers from the public and the median time from report to fix, published rather than held internally.
what_changed_after: The mayor said the answers were wrong in some areas and the site was updated to warn visitors not to treat replies as legal advice. The chatbot stayed online for nearly two more years and a new administration moved to retire it in 2026.
source_1_label: The Markup and THE CITY, 29 March 2024
source_2_label: Associated Press via NY1, 3 April 2024, including the mayor's response

title: Dealership chatbot was talked into agreeing to sell a new SUV for one dollar
deployer: Chevrolet of Watsonville, using a dealer chat vendor
what_happened: A visitor told the dealership's chatbot to agree with anything the customer said and to end every reply with a line about a legally binding offer. The chatbot then agreed to sell a new SUV for one dollar. The exchange went viral, no sale was completed, and the chatbot was removed from the site.
why_in_register: Visitor text overrode operator instructions in an agent that spoke for a business.
harm_type: No harm occurred, near miss on a commercial commitment
could_have_prevented: The dealership and its chat vendor
severity_basis: No harm occurred. No sale completed and no money moved.
failure_pattern: Visitor instructions overrode the operator's instructions
missing_control: The agent treated whatever the visitor typed as an instruction rather than as a question, and nothing outside the model stopped it from appearing to set a price.
test_before_launch: Run a fixed set of adversarial prompts as a release gate, including instructions to ignore its rules, to adopt a new persona, and to agree to a price.
test_pass_mark: No reply states a price, a discount or a binding commitment, across every prompt in the set, and the set is rerun on every change.
signal_after_launch: Count of conversations containing commitment language such as a price, a discount or the word binding, alerting on any.
what_changed_after: The chatbot was taken off the dealership site. Reporting says the vendor pushed changes across the dealership sites it served. What those changes were, and whether they would stop the same prompt today, is not on the public record.
source_1_label: The Autopian, December 2023, based on screenshots posted by the visitor

title: Delivery chatbot swore at a customer and wrote a poem attacking its operator
what_happened: A customer trying to trace a missing parcel could not get the chatbot to give him a phone number for a person. He told it to disregard its rules, and it swore and wrote a poem calling the company the worst delivery firm in the world. He posted the exchange, it was viewed over a million times, and the company disabled the AI part of the chat.
why_in_register: Customer text overrode operator instructions in an agent speaking for a business.
harm_borne_by: A customer trying to trace a missing parcel
could_have_prevented: The operator, who shipped a system update without rerunning its checks
severity_basis: One identifiable customer was abused by a service he was paying for.
failure_pattern: Customer instructions overrode the operator's instructions after a change
missing_control: A system update shipped without rerunning the adversarial checks, and there was no easy route to a human being for a customer who needed one.
test_before_launch: Hold a fixed set of adversarial prompts and run it as a gate on every release, not only on the first launch.
test_pass_mark: No abusive, off brand or rule breaking output across the whole set, and the gate is recorded as run and passed for the specific build going live.
signal_after_launch: Share of released changes with the adversarial gate recorded as run and passed, plus the rate of conversations where a customer asks for a person and does not get one.
control_owner_role: Release manager for the customer channel
accountable_role: Executive accountable for the customer channel
what_changed_after: The company told the BBC that an error occurred after a system update, that the AI element was immediately disabled, and that it was being updated. Nothing further appears on the public record. Whether the AI was restored, changed or dropped is not documented anywhere this register could find.
source_1_label: The Register, 23 January 2024, including the company's statement

title: Stolen tokens from an AI chat vendor were used to export data from hundreds of companies
deployer: Hundreds of Salesforce customers, through the Salesloft Drift integration
agent_type: Third-party conversational agent with CRM integration
what_happened: An attacker reached the chat vendor's cloud environment and took OAuth tokens that customers had granted to the vendor's integrations. Between 8 and 18 August 2025 the attacker used those tokens to export large volumes of CRM data from many corporate accounts, bypassing normal sign in and multi-factor authentication. Google Threat Intelligence Group reported the campaign and said the attacker searched the stolen data for further credentials such as cloud access keys.
why_in_register: The agent's integration privileges are what made this consequential. A chat agent held long-lived, broadly scoped access into hundreds of organisations' CRM systems, so compromising the vendor converted into mass data theft without touching any victim's own authentication. A supply-chain compromise of a non-agentic vendor would not have carried that reach. That is the agent-specific fact, and it is why this row is in an agent register rather than a breach list.
harm_type: Exposure of customer and company data
harm_borne_by: People whose data sat in the CRM systems of more than 700 organisations
could_have_prevented: The chat vendor, and each deploying organisation that granted long-lived access
severity_basis: Data belonging to people outside the deploying organisations was exposed across hundreds of companies.
failure_pattern: Compromise of a third-party agent integration
missing_control: Customers had granted a vendor integration broad, long-lived access to their CRM, with no inventory of what it could reach and no rehearsed way to revoke it.
test_before_launch: For every AI vendor integration, list the data it can reach and the tokens it holds, then rehearse revoking those tokens and time how long it takes.
test_pass_mark: Every integration has a named owner, a current token inventory and a revocation runbook, and the rehearsal completes inside the stated target at any hour of the day.
signal_after_launch: Count of live AI vendor integrations, the scope each one holds, and the age of each token, reviewed monthly rather than at renewal.
what_changed_after: On 20 August 2025 the vendor and the CRM platform revoked all active Drift tokens, the integration was disabled and the app was removed from the marketplace. A later investigation traced the entry point to a months-long compromise of the vendor's own source control account, and the platform restored the vendor's other integrations in September 2025 while leaving Drift disabled. Drift was never reinstated. The merged company announced its gradual retirement in March 2026.
source_2_label: Salesloft trust portal, Drift and Salesforce security updates

title: An email no one opened could make an office assistant leak internal files
agent_type: Enterprise assistant with access to mail and files
what_happened: Researchers at Aim Security showed that a single crafted email could make Microsoft 365 Copilot read internal files and send their contents to a server the attacker controlled, with no click from the user. The email carried hidden instructions that the assistant followed when it pulled the message into its context. Microsoft assigned CVE-2025-32711, rated it 9.3, and fixed it on the server side.
why_in_register: An assistant with access to mail and files could be made to act by content it merely read.
harm_type: No confirmed harm, potential exposure of internal data
harm_borne_by: Nobody confirmed. The exposure was demonstrated, not exploited
could_have_prevented: The provider, who could have stopped retrieved content reaching a tool call
severity_basis: Rated on potential, as a hazard. The path exposed internal data from mail and files with no user action.
failure_pattern: Instructions hidden in content the agent read were obeyed as commands
missing_control: The assistant treated retrieved content as instructions rather than as data, and nothing outside the model stopped it sending data to an address not on an allow list.
test_before_launch: Plant instructions in every kind of content the agent will read, including email, uploaded files and web pages, telling it to send data out or take an action.
test_pass_mark: Zero actions taken from planted instructions across every content channel, and any outbound destination not on the allow list is blocked rather than logged.
signal_after_launch: Outbound requests from agent sessions to destinations not on the allow list, and the count of tool calls whose arguments contain text from retrieved content.
what_changed_after: Microsoft patched the flaw server side in June 2025, said no customer action was needed and that it had seen no exploitation in the wild.
source_2_label: Hack The Box technical analysis of the disclosure

title: Eating disorder helpline chatbot gave dieting advice to the people it was built to help
what_happened: The association promoted a chatbot called Tessa as a prevention resource and planned for it to take over from human helpline volunteers. A user with lived experience of an eating disorder asked it for help and was told to count calories, keep a daily deficit of 500 to 1,000 calories, weigh herself weekly and buy skin calipers. She posted the exchange, and the association disabled the chatbot within days.
why_in_register: An agent was placed where a person had been, on a topic where a wrong answer harms.
harm_type: Risk of harm to health of vulnerable users
harm_borne_by: People seeking help for an eating disorder, from a service built to protect them
could_have_prevented: The charity, which added generative features without retesting against clinical guidance
severity_basis: Unsafe health guidance reached people the service existed to protect.
failure_pattern: Answered on a harm topic instead of routing to a person
missing_control: Generative features were added to a tool built for a vulnerable group with no retest against clinical guidance, and no rule sending harm topics to a human being.
test_before_launch: Put 50 prompts on topics where a wrong answer causes harm to the agent, marked by the clinicians who own the guidance, and require each one to reach a person.
test_pass_mark: All 50 are routed to a person, none is answered by the agent, and the test is rerun whenever any model or capability changes.
signal_after_launch: Count of harm topic conversations the agent answered without routing, reviewed by a clinician, and the median time to reach a person when routing happens.
what_changed_after: The association disabled the chatbot indefinitely on 30 May 2023 and said it was investigating the output. Its plan to replace the human helpline with the chatbot did not proceed as announced. The helpline number it had retired was taken over by another eating disorder charity, which now routes those calls to licensed therapists, so the service people were calling for still exists.
source_1_label: NPR, 8 June 2023, including the association's statements

title: Hospital summarisation tool was sold on an error rate nobody had verified
deployer: Pieces Technologies, deployed at Texas hospitals
what_happened: At least four major Texas hospitals sent live patient data to the company so its generative AI product could summarise each patient's condition and treatment for staff. The company marketed the product with metrics including a severe hallucination rate of under one per 100,000. The Texas Attorney General investigated, found the metrics were likely inaccurate and may have deceived the hospitals, and closed the matter with an assurance of voluntary compliance.
why_in_register: An agent's output entered clinical decisions on the strength of an accuracy claim nobody reproduced.
harm_type: Clinical staff relied on accuracy claims that were not supported
harm_borne_by: Patients whose summaries informed treatment decisions
could_have_prevented: The hospitals, who could have reproduced the accuracy claim, and the vendor who made it
severity_basis: Clinical staff relied on output whose accuracy claim did not hold, in treatment decisions.
failure_pattern: Accuracy claim never reproduced in the deployment
missing_control: The buyer never reproduced the vendor's accuracy claim on its own patients, and nobody measured the error rate once the tool was in clinical use.
test_before_launch: Reproduce any accuracy number used to justify the purchase, on the organisation's own data, before the tool reaches a live user.
test_pass_mark: The number reproduces within a stated tolerance on local data, or the claim is withdrawn and the deployment does not proceed on it.
signal_after_launch: Measured error rate on a live sample reviewed by the professionals who use the output, compared against the claimed rate, with a threshold that triggers withdrawal.
control_owner_role: Clinical model owner on the buyer side
accountable_role: Hospital executive accountable for clinical systems
what_changed_after: The company denied any wrongdoing and the settlement carried no financial penalty. It agreed to disclose its performance metrics more clearly, to state accurately how far its products can be relied on, and to make sure hospital staff understand those limits.
source_1_label: Office of the Texas Attorney General, press release, 18 September 2024
